intro:
Getting phone orders onto the kitchen display means every confirmed order lands in the kitchen screen as a clean ticket, instead of sitting on a notepad or in someone’s memory. That is the simplest way to keep pickup and delivery orders organized when the phone gets busy.

ROAL does that by answering the call, taking the order from your live menu, and sending a kitchen ticket with the details your staff needs. The owner keeps the restaurant’s existing number, and forwarding can be turned on for all calls or only when busy or unanswered.

sections.h2: What should a phone order ticket send to the kitchen?
sections.body:
A good kitchen ticket should be short, clear, and hard to misread. Your cook does not need the whole call transcript. They need the order, the timing, and the contact details that matter.

Use this as the minimum ticket format:
- Customer name and phone number
- Order type: pickup or delivery
- Items, sizes, modifiers, and notes
- Ready time or promised time
- Any special instructions for staff

Example ticket:
| Field | Example |
|---|---|
| Name | Maria S. |
| Phone | 201-555-0148 |
| Order type | Pickup |
| Items | Large pepperoni pizza, no onions; side salad |
| Notes | Cut pizza into squares |
| Ready time | 25 minutes |

If you already use a kitchen display system, ask one simple question: “Can the person on the phone create a ticket the kitchen can read in five seconds?” If the answer is no, the setup is too messy. ROAL sends a clean ticket to the kitchen screen after confirming the order, which is exactly what busy line cooks need.

sections.h2: How do I connect my restaurant phone to the kitchen screen?
sections.body:
The phone side and the kitchen side have to meet somewhere simple. In most restaurants, that means forwarding the existing restaurant number to the phone host, then letting the host send the confirmed order to the kitchen screen.

A practical setup looks like this:
1. Decide which calls should go to the host: all calls, or only busy and unanswered calls.
2. Confirm the forward code with your carrier or phone system.
3. Test a real call and place a small sample order.
4. Watch the ticket appear on the kitchen screen.
5. Make sure the staff can read items, modifiers, and ready time at a glance.

Phone forwarding codes vary, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off. On some GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless often uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically once the owner claims the host, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

sections.h2: What does a clean phone order ticket look like in real life?
sections.body:
Kitchen tickets fail when they are too long, too vague, or full of extra words. A clean ticket should make the next action obvious: start the pizza, pack the sandwich, mark the order ready.

Here is a worked example you can copy for your own menu:
- Restaurant: family pizza shop
- Order: 1 large cheese pizza, 1 medium meat lovers pizza, 2 sodas
- Modifiers: cheese pizza well done, meat lovers no mushrooms
- Notes: call upon arrival for pickup
- Ready time: 20 minutes

Now compare that with a messy version:
- “Caller wants food for later, maybe around 20 minutes, and said something about the pizza being crispy.”

The first version is usable. The second one creates questions at the make line. That is why a kitchen display should show the order in a format that matches how your staff cooks and packs food.

If you use ROAL, the host confirms the order back on the call before the ticket goes to the kitchen screen. It takes items, sizes, modifiers, notes, name, phone, and ready time, which helps reduce back-and-forth at the counter.

sections.h2: How do I handle sold-out items, allergies, and special requests?
sections.body:
The kitchen display should not become a dumping ground for every question. Some calls need staff attention, not an automatic ticket. That includes allergy-sensitive questions, catering requests, complaints, and manager requests.

Use a simple rule:
- Routine order details go to the kitchen screen.
- Sensitive or unusual questions go to staff with a summary.

Example phone lines you can use:
- “Let me check that with the kitchen before I confirm it.”
- “I’m going to send that request to the team and have them review it.”
- “For allergy questions, I’ll get the staff member who handles that.”

That split matters because the kitchen needs speed, but it also needs accuracy. ROAL does not offer items marked sold out. It can hand off catering, complaints, allergy-sensitive questions, and manager requests to staff with a summary. That way, your screen stays clean and your team only sees what they actually need to act on.

Simple checklist before you go live:
- Mark sold-out items in your menu editor
- Decide who handles allergy questions
- Decide who gets manager calls
- Make sure the kitchen screen is checked during rush periods

sections.h2: What should I train staff to watch for on day one?
sections.body:
The first day matters because the kitchen screen is only useful if the team trusts it. Keep the training short and practical.

Train staff on these five things:
1. Where to look for new tickets.
2. How to tell a new ticket from one already preparing.
3. Who marks an order ready.
4. What to do when a ticket looks wrong.
5. Who handles a call summary that was sent to staff instead of the kitchen.

A useful line for the shift lead is: “If the ticket is on the screen, make it. If it looks wrong, flag it right away.” That keeps the team focused.

Also decide who owns menu updates. If a price changes, a topping runs out, or hours change, the menu and hours should be corrected fast so the phone host stays current. ROAL includes a menu editor, hours, FAQs, upsell suggestions, call history with transcripts and recordings, and multi-location menus in the dashboard.

Keep a small opening checklist near the register:
- Kitchen screen on
- Tickets showing in the right order
- Sold-out items updated
- Hours correct
- One person assigned to check call handoffs

sections.h2: How do I set this up without making the phone messy?
sections.body:
Start small and keep the call flow simple. Your goal is not to sound fancy. Your goal is to get the order into the kitchen cleanly.

A practical setup plan:
1. Paste your restaurant website, Google Maps link, or “Name, City” into the setup page.
2. Let ROAL read the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages.
3. Test-call it in the browser before going live.
4. Claim the host and forward the existing number to it.
5. Place one real order and confirm the ticket appears on the kitchen screen.

You can also upload a menu in any format. The owner picks the host’s voice and name, and questions the host could not answer land in an inbox. Once you answer them, the host learns from then on.
